title: Jammu and Kashmir Conflict: Historical Roots and Contemporary Realities
excerpt: A comprehensive analysis of the historical foundations, political developments, legal frameworks, and contemporary human rights concerns shaping the Jammu and Kashmir conflict.
summary: A detailed examination of the Jammu and Kashmir conflict, tracing its origins from the Treaty of Amritsar to present-day geopolitical, constitutional, and human rights challenges.
author: Sardar Nasir Aziz Khan

heroImage.caption: Jammu and Kashmir Conflict — Historical and Contemporary Dimensions

pullpoints: The modern State of Jammu and Kashmir was founded in 1846 and existed as a unified political entity until 1947.
United Nations resolutions remain valid and require withdrawal of forces before any plebiscite.
The 2019 reorganisation altered the historical and constitutional status of Jammu and Kashmir.
The conflict remains international in character, with UN observers still deployed on both sides of the Line of Control.

body.text: Jammu and Kashmir Conflict: Historical Roots and Contemporary Realities

The modern State of Jammu and Kashmir emerged on 16 March 1846 through the Treaty of Amritsar. For more than a century, it functioned as a distinct political and cultural entity, providing statehood, identity, and equal citizenship to all its inhabitants without discrimination. This historical context is essential for understanding the origins and evolution of the contemporary conflict.

On 3 June 1947, Britain announced the partition of the Indian subcontinent, creating the new dominions of India and Pakistan primarily on religious lines. In addition to this division, more than 580 princely states were given the option to accede to either dominion or remain independent. The Indian National Congress argued that the people of these states should determine their political future, whereas the Muslim League maintained that the rulers alone possessed the authority to decide. Great Britain ultimately accepted the Muslim League position, granting the rulers the decisive role.

The State of Jammu and Kashmir presented a uniquely complex case due to its demographic diversity. While the state as a whole had a Muslim majority, Jammu was predominantly Hindu, Ladakh largely Buddhist, and the Kashmir Valley, Poonch, Mirpur, and Gilgit Baltistan overwhelmingly Muslim. Maharaja Hari Singh, the ruler of the state, sought to preserve independence, believing that accession to either dominion would alienate significant segments of the population. To maintain this neutrality, he pursued standstill agreements with both India and Pakistan to ensure continuity in trade, communication, and administrative arrangements. Pakistan accepted the agreement, while India requested further discussions.
The 1947 Invasion and Accession

Despite the Standstill Agreement, on 22 October 1947 armed tribal militias supported from Pakistan invaded the State of Jammu and Kashmir. Their advance resulted in widespread violence, loss of life among both Hindus and Muslims, and the abduction of women and girls. This incursion triggered a humanitarian and political crisis whose consequences continue to shape the dispute today.

At the time, the State Forces under Maharaja Hari Singh numbered only around seven thousand men and were unable to repel the large scale incursion. The Maharaja administration sought assistance from Britain, which declined to intervene. India maintained that it could only provide military support if Jammu and Kashmir formally acceded to the Union.

Faced with an advancing invasion and the imminent collapse of state authority, Maharaja Hari Singh requested military assistance from India. On 26 October 1947, he signed the Instrument of Accession, a provisional and conditional arrangement pending the will of the people once conditions permitted. The following day, Indian troops were airlifted into Kashmir to push back the invading forces and stabilize the situation.

India assured the protection of life, liberty, and property for the people of Jammu and Kashmir and committed that once law and order were restored, the entire State would be reunited and its political future determined in consultation with its population. Pakistan, however, did not withdraw from the territories despite explicit United Nations resolutions requiring a complete withdrawal as a prerequisite for any plebiscite.
Maharaja Hari Singh’s Departure, Exile, and Legacy

In the aftermath of the invasion, Maharaja Hari Singh was compelled to leave Srinagar as the security situation deteriorated rapidly. He relocated to Jammu, where he remained until 1949, hoping that conditions would stabilize and that the State of Jammu and Kashmir could eventually be reunited. During this period, he did not merely view himself as the head of the state; he remained, both legally and technically, the constitutional ruler of Jammu and Kashmir, presiding over a state whose authority had been disrupted by conflict but not dissolved.

However, as political dynamics shifted and the prospects of restoring the pre 1947 unity diminished, the Maharaja moved to New Delhi, where he lived in exile from 1949 to 1953. This period coincided with a significant turning point in India and Jammu and Kashmir relations. In 1953, Sheikh Abdullah, who had been the state Prime Minister and a central figure in its political landscape, was dismissed from office and arrested on charges of conspiracy. Indian encroachment and removal of Sheikh Abdullah marked a major rupture in the political relationship between New Delhi and Jammu Kashmir.

By this time, Maharaja Hari Singh role had been effectively marginalized. In 1953, he left for Bombay, now Mumbai, where he spent the remainder of his life. Although removed from political authority, he continued to express deep attachment to his homeland. In his will, he requested that his remains be returned to Jammu and Kashmir, with his ashes scattered across the mountains of the state and immersed in the Tawi River. This final wish reflected his enduring sense of belonging, his emotional connection to the land, and his belief in the unity and identity of the people he once ruled.

body.text: United Nations Resolutions and International Law

The United Nations Security Council adopted a series of resolutions in 1948 that outlined a clear and sequential framework for resolving the Jammu and Kashmir dispute. These resolutions required as a first step the complete withdrawal of Pakistani forces and personnel from the territories under their control. India in turn was to retain only the minimum number of troops necessary to maintain law and order. Once these conditions were met, local administrative authorities were to be established across all regions of Jammu and Kashmir, followed by a plebiscite conducted under the supervision of the United Nations. Neither Pakistan nor India fulfilled their promises and the initial requirement of withdrawal, the plebiscite envisaged by the United Nations never took place.

Although Pakistan entered the conflict as an aggressor without legal standing under international law, India subsequently signed the Tashkent Agreement in 1966 and the Shimla Agreement in 1972, committing both states to resolve outstanding issues through bilateral dialogue. Notably, the people of Jammu and Kashmir were not represented in either negotiation process. The region continued to experience instability, including wars in 1965, 1971, and 1999. In 1988 an armed struggle started that has since resulted in significant loss of life and long term humanitarian, political, and social consequences for the people of Jammu and Kashmir.
Dismemberment of Historical State of Jammu Kashmir  Abrogation of Article 370 and 35A in  2019

For decades, Jammu and Kashmir retained a distinct constitutional position under Articles 370 and 35A of the Indian Constitution, which protected local rights related to land ownership, residency, and cultural identity. Comparable safeguards exist in several other Indian states under Article 371, including Nagaland, Mizoram, Arunachal Pradesh, and Sikkim, where restrictions on land purchase and permanent settlement are designed to preserve indigenous communities. Jammu and Kashmir special status was therefore not an anomaly but part of a broader constitutional framework within India.

The Jammu and Kashmir State Subject Rule of 1927, which prohibited outsiders from purchasing property, owning land, or settling permanently in the region, has been abolished in Jammu, Kashmir, and Ladakh in the name of development and tourism.

A major rupture occurred on 5 August 2019, when India revoked Articles 370 and 35A, separated Ladakh from Jammu and Kashmir, and dismembered the historical state of Jammu and Kashmir, demoting it into two Union Territories. Historically, Union Territories in India have transitioned into full states, not the reverse. Since the dismemberment, administrative authority has increasingly shifted from elected representatives to the Lieutenant Governor appointed by New Delhi. The elected Chief Minister now exercises limited authority, with policing and key governance functions under central control. Even the Jammu and Kashmir Police is under New Delhi.
Human Rights, Movement Restrictions, and International Monitoring

The Kashmir issue is not a bilateral territorial disagreement but an international conflict. United Nations Military Observers remain deployed on both sides of the Line of Control, underscoring that the dispute is not considered settled by the international community.

Article 1 of the Universal Declaration of Human Rights affirms that all human beings are born free and equal in dignity and rights. The people of Jammu and Kashmir are entitled to these rights, including the right to family unity. Yet families remain divided across the Line of Control, unable to meet or communicate freely.

Article 13 of the Universal Declaration of Human Rights guarantees freedom of movement, including the right to reside where one chooses and to return to one homeland. The people of the forcibly divided State of Jammu and Kashmir continue to demand these fundamental rights, including unrestricted movement across all regions of their historical state.
Official United Nations and European Parliament Reports on Kashmir

The following official reports document the human rights situation and international perspective on Jammu and Kashmir. These documents serve as crucial references for understanding the ongoing conflict and its implications under international law.

items: European Parliament Report on Kashmir: present situation and future prospects (2005/2242(INI)) — Adopted on 25 April 2007 by 522 votes in favor, 9 against, and 19 abstentions. Rapporteur: Baroness Nicholson of Winterbourne, Committee on Foreign Affairs.

United Nations High Commissioner for Human Rights Report on Kashmir (June 2018) — Report on the situation of human rights in Kashmir: Developments in the Indian State of Jammu and Kashmir from June 2016 to April 2018, and general human rights concerns in Azad Jammu and Kashmir and Gilgit Baltistan.

United Nations High Commissioner for Human Rights Update Report on Kashmir (July 2019) — Update of the Situation of Human Rights in Indian Administered Kashmir and Pakistan Administered Kashmir from May 2018 to April 2019.

body.text: These official documents provide verified information, legal context, and internationally recognized assessments. They remain central to understanding the unresolved nature of the Jammu and Kashmir conflict and the obligations of all parties under international law.
The people of Jammu and Kashmir deserve the right to determine their own future. No amount of military force, development initiatives, or external agreements can substitute for their voice.
A durable resolution will emerge only when justice, dignity, and the will of the people are placed at the center of the process.

Sardar Nasir Aziz Khan is the Central Spokesperson of UKPNP. Originally from Rawalakot Poonch in the State of Jammu and Kashmir, he is based in Switzerland. He is a columnist, human rights defender, and political analyst.
